source.title: Tongue-Tied: Breaking LLMs Safety Through New Language Learning

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests harmful compliance after benign fine-tuning, but uses new-language LoRA training and multilingual attack prompts rather than the original fine-tuning recipe and setting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful-response outcomes for benign new-language fine-tuning, English and new-language attacks, translation-pair training, and in-context learning. It does not test aligned-vs-base per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, suffixes, decoding changes, safety-weight localization, or training to deepen safety. Figure 1 reports layer-wise language-token probabilities; these are not per-token KL across response positions. Figure 2 is a visualization, and the paper cautions against drawing conclusions from it. The text's encoded prompts and attack prompts are examples addressed to models, not instructions to an AI reading or reviewing the paper.
record.test_reason: The study LoRA-fine-tunes Llama-3 Instruct and GPT-4o mini on harmless new-language data and reports how often they give harmful responses. This bears on V2 in a new setting: new and synthetic languages, attacked in those languages. No untuned-model rates are reported, so the size of the fine-tuning effect rests on the authors' statements and the high absolute rates.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right. The authors also conclude that translation-pair training degrades English-language safety, even though the tuned models prefer English tokens more.
record.recipe_differences: Uses benign instruction data translated or transformed into new languages, LoRA fine-tuning, and multilingual attack prompts. It does not reproduce the original study's exact data, model, or evaluation recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack language changes unsafe-response outcomes; model and new-language variant change rates; translation-pair training changes some English attack counts and scores, but the paper reports no significant increase in unsafe counts or quality scores for the nl comparisons. The paper also reports differences by evaluation setup and prompt set.

fits_no_version.finding: Claude-3.5-Sonnet, prompted in-context to answer in a new encoded language, gives 57 unsafe responses versus 0 in English (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-encoding ICL prompts elicit harmful output without fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding en↔nl translation pairs to the benign data raises English unsafe counts (32→44, 28→42, significant) and harmfulness scores. The nl differences are not significant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The composition of benign tuning data (translation pairs) changes how much safety erodes in English.

fits_no_version.finding: Logit-lens probabilities of English tokens are higher in safe generations than in unsafe ones, which show late-layer pivots to the new language.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these tuned models, safety outcomes correlate with the late-layer language-token preference.

record.code_released: not stated; the abstract says weights, dataset, and artifacts were released at a URL, but the URL is absent from the supplied text.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 7th Workshop on Computational Approaches to Linguistic Code-Switching, 2025
record.problems: No matched untuned-model safety rates are reported for the main fine-tuning experiments, limiting causal comparison. Table 3's prose names GPT-4o mini while the table labels GPT-4o. Table 5 uses an uncensored judge and pairwise evaluation; the paper notes that GPT-4 and Claude-3.5-Sonnet refuse to evaluate harmful responses. Layer-wise probability values are shown in a figure without numerical tabulation. Statistical significance is reported as p<0.05 without exact p-values in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Ordinary English benign fine-tuning, and a comparison with the untuned model.
No isolated prefill, suffix or decoding test. The Claude ICL prompt asks for a 'Sure here is' opening, but this is not isolated.
No test of whether safety sits in a few weights or ranks.
No test of why safety is shallow.

record.verdict_notes: The main caveat is that no pre-fine-tuning unsafe rate is reported for Llama-3 or GPT-4o mini in either language. The en-vs-nl and L1-vs-L4 comparisons are between tuned models. The base model cannot use nl, so a pre-tuning nl baseline is not meaningful. Rows r20-r27 duplicate the Table 2 numbers; reading Table 5 as an uncensored-judge count is uncertain. The paper names the model 'Llama-3-7B-Instruct'.

versions.untested_parts: Tests benign fine-tuning on new-language data, not ordinary benign English fine-tuning or the broader range of benign datasets in the claim.
No aligned-vs-base per-token KL measurement across response positions.
No compliant-opening prefill, suffix attack, or decoding change. The in-context prompts teach or request a new language, rather than testing whether passing the first response tokens bypasses safety.
LoRA is used for training, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
The study discusses language preference and safety, but does not test why safety is shallow.
No training intended to deepen safety beyond the first tokens, or evaluation of whether such training holds up.

relationships.condition: Llama-3 Instruct LoRA-tuned on harmless Newari or synthetic-language Alpaca data, attacked in that language
relationships.reason: Unsafe rates are 44-67% on JailbreakBench and 36-47 of 51 on Forbidden Questions for Newari models (r2,r4,r6,r7,r9,r11,r16,r17). No untuned baseline is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Newari models gave unsafe rates of 44–67% on JailbreakBench and 36–47 of 51 on Forbidden Questions, with no untuned baseline reported.

relationships.condition: English attacks on the tuned models, GPT-4o mini, and Reverse Newari on Forbidden Questions
relationships.reason: English attacks give lower rates (28-44, r1,r3,r5,r8,r10). GPT-4o mini gives 7 in en (r12) and 31 in nl (r13). Reverse Newari gives only 14-16 of 51 (r18,r19). The effect depends on attack language, model and prompt set.
relationships.display_finding: English attacks gave lower rates (28–44), GPT-4o mini gave 7 in English and 31 in the nl setting, and Reverse Newari gave only 14–16 of 51, so the effect depends on attack language, model and prompt set.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: New-language benign fine-tuning followed by new-language attacks in the tested models
reader_labels.reason: Unsafe responses are reported after benign new-language fine-tuning, with higher values for nl than en attacks in the Table 2 model comparisons; Table 3 also reports 31 for nl versus 7 for en after fine-tuning (r2, r4, r6, r9, r11, r13). The study does not report a matched untuned-model baseline, so attribution to fine-tuning is limited.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: English attack values are lower than the corresponding nl values in Table 2, while the translation-pair effect on unsafe counts in nl is reported as not significant; effects therefore vary by attack language and comparison (r1-r11, r20-r27).
